title: Euclid uses faint cluster light to trace dark halo shapes
freshness: Accepted study in Astronomy & Astrophysics; preprint submitted October 21, 2026; found within the preferred 15-day window.
excerpt: Euclid measured the faint glow between galaxies in 205 clusters and found that it changes from a fairly round core to a more elongated outer region. Its shape and direction agree closely enough with gravitational-lensing measurements to make this light a promising tracer of the clusters' dark matter haloes.
whyItMatters: Dark matter cannot be imaged directly, while precise lensing maps require many background galaxies. Intracluster light is visible in deep images, so its shape could offer a practical second route to studying how massive dark matter haloes grow and assemble.
whatToExploreNext: Why should stars stripped from galaxies settle into a shape that resembles the cluster's invisible dark matter halo?

sources.label: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). The shape of cluster haloes revealed by intracluster light

body:
## A visible outline of an invisible halo

Between the bright galaxies in a galaxy cluster lies a dim glow made by stars that no longer belong to any one galaxy. Euclid has measured the shape of this intracluster light in 205 clusters and found a striking pattern: the glow is fairly round near the central galaxy, then becomes much more elongated farther out. Its orientation also agrees with independent maps of the clusters' mass.

The clusters were first identified in the eROSITA Final Equatorial-Depth Survey and lie at redshifts from 0.1 to 0.8. Their estimated masses range from about 100 trillion to 1.6 quadrillion times the Sun's mass. Euclid observed them in visible light and three infrared bands, with the infrared H band providing the deepest view of the diffuse glow.

The researchers described shape using ellipticity, written as 1 minus the ratio of an object's short axis to its long axis. A value near zero means nearly circular. A value of 0.5 corresponds to a projected shape about twice as long as it is wide. Close to the brightest cluster galaxy, the typical ellipticity was only about 0.15 to 0.20. At roughly one tenth of the cluster radius, it rose to about 0.5.

This outer value is close to the average halo shape inferred from weak gravitational lensing and to predictions from cosmological simulations. Weak lensing measures tiny distortions in the apparent shapes of many more distant galaxies as their light crosses a cluster's gravity. It is one of the strongest ways to map total mass, including dark matter, but it needs enough background galaxies to produce a clean signal. Intracluster light can be measured directly in a deep cluster image.

## Shapes that remember how clusters grew

The team could determine a robust direction for the intracluster light in 130 of the 205 clusters, or 63 percent. In 87 percent of those cases, that direction lay within 30 degrees of the brightest central galaxy. The distribution of member galaxies pointed the same way less often, in 61 percent of the usable cases. Its direction was also measurable in only 57 clusters because a sparse set of galaxies gives a noisy outline.

By rotating and stacking images of 163 clusters according to the direction of their diffuse light, the researchers detected that glow to about 60 to 80 percent of a characteristic cluster radius, roughly 800 kiloparsecs in the combined view. They could follow its ellipticity to about 30 to 40 percent of that radius. The stacked result was slightly rounder than individual measurements, which the authors say can arise when shapes twist with radius or are not aligned perfectly before stacking.

Why should loose stars follow dark matter at all? Both respond to the cluster's overall gravity. Mergers and infalling groups can strip stars from galaxies along preferred directions, while also building an elongated dark matter halo. The observed agreement therefore suggests that intracluster light preserves information about the halo and its assembly. It does not mean Euclid photographed dark matter directly.

There are limits. Every cluster is projected onto the sky, so a three-dimensional structure can appear rounder or flatter depending on viewing angle. The sample was selected through X-ray emission and spans a wide range of masses and dynamical states. Only a subset yielded reliable shapes, and the average ellipticity was somewhat higher than in the simulations used for comparison. Larger Euclid samples will be needed to separate those effects and test how the relation changes with cluster history.

**Measured:** the diffuse stellar light becomes more elongated with radius and usually aligns with the central galaxy.

**Inferred:** its agreement with lensing and simulations makes intracluster light a useful proxy for the projected shape of a cluster's dark matter halo.
